events_chronological: Helicopters spray the city for crop pests through the night, passing over every neighbourhood in the film.
Doctor Neil Hartigan and his wife Bess, a painter, get ready for a dinner party.
The baker Otto Kemp takes an order for a birthday cake for a boy called Charlie Rill.
Charlie is knocked down by a car driven by a waitress called Rhona on his way to school and walks home insisting he is fine.
Charlie collapses into a coma, and his parents Grant and Elaine keep vigil at the hospital.
Grant's estranged father Duff turns up at the hospital and confesses an affair from decades ago.
Unpaid and ignored, the baker starts making anonymous menacing phone calls to the family.
Telephone-sex worker Cheryl talks men through their fantasies from her living room while her husband Stu seethes beside her.
Stu and three friends drive out to fish and find a young woman's body face down in the river.
The men tether the body to the bank and carry on fishing for two more days before telling anyone.
Vern's wife Iris, a party clown, is disgusted when she learns what the men did.
The singer Vida performs nightly in a club while her cellist daughter Bee plays alone at home.
Officer Rowe, cheating on his wife Peg with a woman called Nan, abandons the family dog to cover one of his lies.
Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot, learns she has a new man and saws her furniture to pieces.
Ike and Dot house-sit for the Hartigans and photograph Dot made up as a beaten corpse.
At the dinner party Bess admits to a long-ago nude modelling session and an affair, and Neil makes a scene.
Charlie dies in hospital, and Grant and Elaine go to the bakery to confront Otto, who feeds them warm bread and grieves with them.
Bee finds her mother asleep, closes the garage door and kills herself with the car engine running.
At a picnic in the hills Stu smashes a young woman's head with a rock.
A tremor shakes the entire city, and every death and every wreck is folded into one evening bulletin.
nonlinear_category_reason: Nine strands run concurrently between the night spraying and the earthquake; every scene keeps its own strand's forward order, and the inversions are only between simultaneous households.
syuzhet_notes: The film braids nine loosely connected city stories that run at the same time rather than one after another, cutting between them constantly and often on a sound or a passing car. Because the strands are concurrent, most of the reordering is lateral - the film moves sideways between households rather than backwards in time - with the night spraying at told-order bullet 1 and the earthquake at bullet 20 bracketing everything in between.
fabula_notes: The strands are simultaneous and the film supplies almost no clock times, so the ordering across the three days rests on the few hard markers: the cake is ordered before the accident, the fishing trip runs across a weekend, the earthquake closes everything. The dead woman in the river is never identified or explained, and any connection between her and the last killing is left for the audience to draw.

events.content: All night, low over the roofs, a fleet of machines puts poison on the fruit fly and on everybody's washing, and every household in the film hears the same noise at the same hour.

reader: one event that touches every strand and connects none of them

House-sitting somebody else's good address, they make each other up with bruises and a lot of pale foundation and take pictures of her lying in the hall being dead.

events.content: The ground moves for about eleven seconds. By the evening bulletin the deaths, the wrecks and the woman in the river have all been folded into the same three minutes of news.
